# Introduction

The Reject Inference (RI) problem concerns the challenge of learning from
outcomes that are only observed for accepted applicants, and of using information
from rejected applicants whose outcomes remain unknown. This selective observation
induces acceptance bias and motivates methods for its identification and correction.
Reject Inference has been widely researched for applications in fields like credit
scoring, medical applications or underwriting and rather indirectly from a theoretical
perspective as a missing data problem. Although the research has delivered mixed
results, leading some like @HandHanley1993CanRIWork to question whether RI can even
work, its potential in such high-stakes decision systems keeps driving the search for
this "holy grail".

This work takes in some sense a step backwards in relationship to current literature
and studies RI itself from a fresh perspective. The acceptance bias
occurs because based on (biased) historical data, new acceptance decision are made. This new
accepts become later part of the history on which an institution will base further future
decision on. Therefore, RI constitutes inherently a dynamic problem. Despite that several
authors like @kozdoi_et_al_BE_BASL generate simulation data using such an acceptance loop,
it has not been yet tried to extract information from the dynamic structure of the loop itself.
To do so I follow an intuition: the acceptance bias must be some sort of self-biasing mechanism,
the longer a biased selection mechanism is used, the bias should become worse.



Main contributions expected:

* Measure Theoretic formalization of the RI problem for credit risk as a stochastic
  process introducing a dynamic dimension as methodology to make more explicit all
  assumptions on the DGP for simulation frameworks.
* Simulation framework
  * Types of classifiers evaluated (Accept based classifier, oracle naive, oracle comparable)
  * Sensitivity parameters on strength of MNAR:
    * Correlation of hidden factor
    * Bias percentage
* RL set up:
  * Reward function as "surprise minimizer"
  * "Batch of batches" perspective for optimizing global minimization instead of trying to
    calculate individual rewards.
  * RL Architecture cut for this set up
